what_it_does: Attention — the step where each word in a language model looks up how relevant every other word is — is a major bottleneck at long context lengths. It's slow for two reasons: the running memory store of past words (called the KV cache, a table of key-value vectors the model consults for every new word generated) grows huge, and the mathematical normalization step (softmax, which converts raw scores to probabilities using exponentiation) forces the GPU to use its slow general-purpose cores instead of its fast matrix-multiply units. TurboAttention fixes both problems together, delivering 1.2–1.8x latency speedup and reducing KV cache memory by over 4.4x.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Modern GPUs have two kinds of compute units: fast 'tensor cores' (specialized units for multiplying blocks of numbers together, roughly 30x faster) that only work in 16-bit floating point or 8-bit integer formats, and slow general-purpose 'CUDA cores' that handle arbitrary math including exponentiation. Standard attention (including the widely used FlashAttention algorithm) must call the slow CUDA cores for softmax's exponentiation step, and must expand numbers to 32-bit precision to avoid overflow — wasting most of the GPU's speed advantage. Meanwhile, compressed KV caches (shrinking stored values to 4 or 2 bits) still have to decompress back to 16-bit before doing the attention math, largely erasing the benefit.

FlashQ — quantized attention math. TurboAttention introduces blockwise progressive quantization (BPQ): it takes each small tile of query, key, and value matrices (the chunks that FlashAttention processes one at a time) and immediately compresses them to 8-bit integers using symmetric scaling (dividing by the block's max absolute value). All the big matrix multiplies inside attention now run on tensor cores in 8-bit integer arithmetic — fast. After the computation, key and value tiles are further compressed to 4-bit or 2-bit for storage in the KV cache using channel-wise asymmetric quantization (a finer-grained scheme that sets a separate scale and offset per feature dimension to handle outlier values). A head-wise mixed precision scheme assigns 2-bit compression to the least sensitive attention heads (ranked by a gap×standard-deviation priority score) and 4-bit to the rest, balancing memory savings against accuracy.

SAS — softmax on tensor cores. SAS (Sparse Activated Softmax) replaces the slow FP32 exponentiation with a two-part approximation: a lookup table for the integer part of the exponent (compact because large negative exponents decay to near-zero quickly), and a 3rd-degree polynomial fit for the fractional part, both operated in 16-bit on tensor cores. Attention scores below a threshold are set to exactly zero (the 'sparse' part), keeping the lookup table small and reducing computation.

The key design choice. By running all matrix multiplies in 8-bit integer and softmax in 16-bit on tensor cores, the entire attention computation stays on the fast path. No step needs to leave the tensor cores for CUDA cores.

The result. On an NVIDIA A100 GPU running Phi3-Medium, LLaMA3-8B, and Qwen2-7B, TurboAttention achieves up to 1.8x prefill speedup and 1.7x decode speedup versus FlashAttention2 (FP16 baseline), up to 2.37x higher maximum throughput, and near-lossless accuracy on math reasoning and symbolic reasoning benchmarks at 4-bit KV cache compression.
